caption_gt: Histopathologic features of keratoacanthoma, observed at 40× magnification. This image, stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), illustrates characteristic features of keratoacanthoma across its various developmental and regressive phases. The early proliferation phase of keratoacanthoma is characterized by a small, primarily solid tumor containing several distinct infundibulocystic structures that have not yet coalesced into a central keratin plug. These structures include islands of laminated keratin with a ground-glass appearance, which may merge. Nuclear atypia is typically absent within the center of these structures, though some peripheral atypia may be allowed, and generally becomes less prominent with maturation. Inflammation, involving histiocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, and plasma cells, may also be present. The maturation phase demonstrates more defined features, such as an exo–endophytic squamous proliferation with a central keratin plug, overhanging epithelial lips, and compact keratinization. Significant variability of cellular appearance and atypia can be observed, with most pleomorphic cells located in the most distant fringes. The regression phase presents with a “hollowing out” of the lesion, losing its central keratin plug, and beginning to resemble an empty bowl as the keratin clears and the epithelium thins. This phase is also marked by perilesional dermal inflammation, particularly lymphocytic infiltrate, and increasing cicatricial fibrosis.
